issues.legal_issue: Convictions for conspiracy, cheating, and criminal misconduct were sustainable where a public servant and a private beneficiary acted together to disburse loans dishonestly without required safeguards and the beneficiary obtained the proceeds.
material_facts: The branch manager disbursed loan proceeds to the private beneficiary despite the absence of required employer undertakings, competent salary-deduction authorizations, pre-inspection reports, and security for the relevant borrowers.
The manager falsely represented that required undertakings had been obtained, and loans were processed and disbursed without ensuring that borrowers had accounts for repayment.
The beneficiary received the loan proceeds, but plots were not transferred to many borrowers and no collateral security was created for those loans.
Evidence showed payments from the beneficiary to the manager, meetings between them, and the transfer of loan proceeds to the beneficiary’s account.
The prosecution also relied on oral and documentary evidence, while the defence did not establish that the required conditions had been met.
issues.conclusion: The evidence established the charges beyond reasonable doubt, and the convictions for conspiracy and cheating, and the manager’s conviction for criminal misconduct, were rightly confirmed.
issues.legal_principle: The offences were assessed under Sections 120-B and 420 of the Indian Penal Code and Sections 13(1)(d) and 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The prosecution had to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt; the accused could establish a defence on a preponderance of probabilities (T. Subramanian v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2006) 1 SCC 401). A court may draw a factual presumption from proved facts (M. Narsinga Rao v. State of Andhra Pradesh, (2001) 1 SCC 691). Criminal misconduct requires proof that a public servant abused official position or used corrupt or illegal means to obtain a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage for himself or another.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.required_loan_safeguards_were_bypassed: An official responsible for approving or disbursing loans proceeded without safeguards required to protect repayment or secure the loans.
predicates.loan_proceeds_were_diverted_to_beneficia: Loan proceeds intended for specified borrowers or purposes were credited to a beneficiary who did not provide the promised property or security for some of the loans.
predicates.false_assurances_were_made: An accused falsely represented that required conditions for the loans had been satisfied.
predicates.payments_were_made_between_colluding_par: Evidence showed payments between participants who acted together in the loan scheme.

issues.definition: When a criminal conviction appeal concerns a loan scheme in which required safeguards were bypassed and proceeds went to a beneficiary, false assurances or payments between colluding participants support upholding the conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A criminal conspiracy may be proved by circumstantial evidence establishing a meeting of minds to commit an illegal act or to act by illegal means.
material_facts: The manager and beneficiary met on several occasions.
Evidence showed that the beneficiary paid money to the manager on multiple occasions.
The manager sanctioned loans whose proceeds were transferred to the beneficiary’s account.
The circumstances surrounding the loans and the absence of promised plots and security supported an inference that the two acted together.
issues.conclusion: The proved circumstances permitted the Court to infer that the manager and beneficiary had conspired.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 120-A of the Indian Penal Code, conspiracy requires a meeting of minds of two or more persons to do, or cause to be done, an illegal act or an act by illegal means. Because conspiracy is generally hatched in secrecy, substantial direct evidence may not be available and the offence may be proved by circumstantial evidence. The Court applied the principles discussed in State of Madhya Pradesh v. Sheetla Sahai, (2009) 8 SCC 617.

predicates.criminal_conspiracy_prosecution: The proceeding alleges that two or more people agreed to pursue an illegal act or an act by illegal means.
predicates.direct_evidence_of_agreement_is_unavaila: The alleged agreement was made secretly and no substantial direct evidence of the agreement is available.
predicates.circumstantial_evidence_shows_joint_acti: Evidence shows coordinated conduct, such as repeated meetings, transfers of proceeds, or payments between the alleged participants.

issues.definition: In a conspiracy prosecution, when direct evidence of the agreement is unavailable, circumstantial evidence of coordinated conduct may establish the conspiracy.

issues.legal_issue: Civil recovery proceedings and decrees do not, by themselves, override or preclude a criminal prosecution arising from the same transactions.
material_facts: The bank obtained decrees against borrowers for repayment of the loans, including simple money decrees and mortgage decrees.
The decrees did not result in full repayment; only one borrower had liquidated the loan, and the bank had suffered a loss of interest.
The criminal prosecution concerned the alleged dishonest loan scheme and the conduct of the accused, rather than merely the borrowers’ civil liability for repayment.
issues.conclusion: The civil decrees did not defeat or override the criminal prosecution.
issues.legal_principle: A civil claim or decree does not override a criminal prosecution. The Court relied on K.G. Premshanker v. Inspector of Police, (2002) 8 SCC 87, and R. Venkatkrishnan v. CBI, (2009) 11 SCC 737.

predicates.criminal_prosecution_arises_from_transac: A criminal prosecution concerns transactions for which a civil recovery claim or proceeding also exists.
predicates.civil_decree_does_not_resolve_criminal_l: The civil decree addresses recovery but does not determine whether the accused committed the alleged criminal acts.

issues.definition: When civil recovery concerns the same transactions but does not determine criminal liability, the civil proceeding does not bar the criminal prosecution.

issues.legal_issue: Irregularities or deficiencies in an investigation do not invalidate a prosecution when sufficient evidence establishes its essential factual foundation.
material_facts: The accused alleged irregularities or deficiencies in the investigation.
The prosecution had produced oral and documentary evidence that the Court found sufficient to establish the essential facts of the charges.
issues.conclusion: The alleged investigative deficiencies did not warrant setting aside the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: Investigative irregularities are not invariably fatal. If sufficient evidence establishes the substratum of the prosecution case, deficiencies that do not affect that foundation should not determine the outcome. The Court relied on Kashinath Mondal v. State of West Bengal, (2012) 7 SCC 699.

predicates.criminal_case_under_review: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the validity of the prosecution is challenged.
predicates.sufficient_evidence_establishes_prosecut: The prosecution has produced sufficient evidence to establish the essential facts supporting its case.
predicates.investigative_defect_does_not_affect_tha: An alleged investigative irregularity does not undermine the essential factual foundation established by the evidence.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, an investigative irregularity that leaves the evidential foundation intact does not invalidate the prosecution.

issues.legal_issue: An accused’s examination answers may be considered with the prosecution evidence, but they cannot alone supply the basis for conviction.
material_facts: The accused argued that answers given during examination under the criminal procedure code could not form the basis for conviction.
The prosecution had produced independent oral and documentary evidence establishing the chain of events.
The Court considered the accused’s answers alongside that prosecution evidence.
issues.conclusion: The accused’s answers were a relevant consideration because the prosecution had independently established the chain of events.
issues.legal_principle: Answers given by an accused during examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, may be relevant for the court’s consideration, particularly where the prosecution has established the chain of events; they are not the sole basis for conviction in this case.

predicates.criminal_case_under_review: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the evidential value of the accused’s examination answers is disputed.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_establishes_chain_o: Evidence independent of the accused’s answers establishes the sequence of events supporting the prosecution case.
predicates.accused_examination_answers_are_consider: The court assesses the accused’s answers alongside, rather than instead of, the prosecution evidence.

issues.definition: When independent prosecution evidence establishes the chain of events, the accused’s examination answers may be considered together with that evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A prior service dismissal did not make the criminal prosecution unwarranted in the circumstances where there was no honourable acquittal and the criminal conviction was under challenge.
material_facts: The manager argued that he had already been dismissed from service and that criminal prosecution on the same facts was therefore impermissible.
The cited earlier decision concerned a departmental inquiry following an acquittal while proceedings challenging dismissal were pending.
The accused in this case had not been honourably acquitted; the criminal courts had convicted him.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decision did not assist the manager, and the prior service dismissal did not warrant setting aside the criminal conviction.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished State Bank of Hyderabad v. P. Kata Rao, (2008) 15 SCC 657, on its facts, including the honourable acquittal involved there, and stated that each cause must be determined on its own facts.

predicates.criminal_prosecution_challenged_after_se: An accused relies on a prior dismissal from employment to challenge a criminal prosecution based on related facts.
predicates.no_honourable_acquittal_has_occurred: The accused has not been honourably acquitted in the criminal proceeding.

issues.definition: A prior service dismissal, without an honourable acquittal, does not by itself defeat a criminal prosecution.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court would not use its discretionary jurisdiction to disturb concurrent convictions supported by acceptable oral and documentary evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court had both convicted the accused on the charges upheld in the appeals.
The concurrent findings rested on oral and documentary evidence that the Supreme Court found acceptable.
The accused challenged those findings in appeals brought by special leave.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere under Article 136 of the Constitution and dismissed both appeals.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution of India, the Court declined to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction where concurrent findings of conviction were based on acceptable evidence.

predicates.special_leave_criminal_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal before the Supreme Court brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_convictions_are_supported_by_: The lower courts made concurrent findings of guilt supported by acceptable oral or documentary evidence.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal by special leave, concurrent convictions supported by acceptable evidence result in the Supreme Court declining to interfere.
